candidate_tradeoffs.name: First-party native Web Platform client
strengths: zero third-party UI runtime and smallest compared product-runtime supply-chain surface
direct use of URL/History, AbortController and standards-based DOM primitives preserves backend neutrality
representative CMDR benchmark shows very low incremental update cost for frequent Event Search state changes
CSP and Trusted Types can be layered without framework-specific escaping or hydration semantics
weaknesses: CMDR must own state discipline, rendering conventions, virtualization and component lifecycle engineering
accessibility remains an explicit engineering obligation rather than an automatic framework property

candidate_tradeoffs.name: Server-rendered semantic HTML with first-party progressive enhancement
strengths: semantic HTML and low client runtime provide a strong accessibility and graceful-degradation foundation
representative benchmark shows competitive initial fragment readiness
weaknesses: full-fragment replacement is materially more expensive than bounded incremental updates in the representative Event Search workload
highly interactive search state risks being split across server navigation and enhanced client state

candidate_tradeoffs.name: Lit Web Components runtime
strengths: declarative Web Components model with targeted updates and relatively small runtime
keeps browser standards visible at component boundaries
weaknesses: adds a third-party product-runtime dependency despite CMDR being able to implement the required primitives natively
adds ongoing dependency review, update and supply-chain obligations

candidate_tradeoffs.name: Svelte compiled component architecture
strengths: compiler-oriented reactivity can reduce manual rendering boilerplate
generated client code can perform fine-grained updates
weaknesses: adds a third-party compiler/toolchain and framework-generated semantics that require upgrade revalidation
framework coupling is unnecessary for the currently bounded Event Search requirements

candidate_tradeoffs.name: React runtime architecture
strengths: mature rich-interaction model and broad engineering ecosystem
supports client and server rendering patterns
weaknesses: largest compared third-party runtime and framework-specific rendering surface
hydration and framework-specific state semantics add failure modes that do not advance CMDR's backend-neutral contract

benchmarks.workload: Event Search synthetic DOM workload with 250 visible forensic-result rows, 30 initial-render samples per run, 160 state updates per run, 12 incrementally mutated rows per native update, and complete 250-row fragment replacement for the server-progressive alternative; seven repeated runs
benchmarks.environment: Linux x86_64; Chrome/Chromium 144.0.7559.96 headless; V8 14.4.258.22; GPU disabled; local about:blank DevTools Protocol execution; no network and no third-party JavaScript runtime
benchmarks.dataset_scale: 250 rendered result rows; 160 update operations per run; seven independent measurement runs after warm-up

adversarial_reviews.hypothesis: A first-party native Web architecture will fail CMDR's Event Search requirements because framework-free state/rendering increases security, accessibility, deep-link consistency and performance risk beyond the benefits of eliminating a UI runtime dependency.
falsification_attempts: compare initial-render and repeated state-update costs against the server-progressive first-party alternative under a representative 250-row Event Search workload
challenge the architecture against DOM-XSS sinks and require safe DOM APIs plus CSP, with Trusted Types treated only as defense in depth
challenge deep-link determinism by requiring URL/History state for query, scope, filters and return context rather than hidden framework state
challenge accessibility by requiring native semantic controls by default and explicit keyboard/focus semantics for any custom element
challenge failure-state completeness against Loading, Empty, Partial, Error, Offline and Permission denied states from INV-EVS-001
challenge backend neutrality by forbidding final query dialect, index, storage, transport-provider and OPEN-013 Case-link assumptions from the frontend architecture
challenge maintainability and supply-chain assumptions against Lit, Svelte and React evidence rather than assuming zero-runtime is automatically simpler
counter_evidence: server-progressive rendering had a lower median p95 initial-fragment cost in the representative benchmark
native Web requires CMDR to own more state/rendering/virtualization conventions and tests
Lit and Svelte can reduce declarative-reactivity boilerplate even though they add dependency/toolchain surface
